The 10,227th meeting of the Security Council is called to order. The provisional agenda for this meeting is: Maintenance of peace and security of Ukraine. The agenda is adopted. I would like to welcome very warmly the distinguished Presidents, Prime Minister and Ministers present in the Security Council Chamber. Your presence today underscores the importance of the subject matter under discussion. In accordance with Rule 37 of the Council's Provisional Rules of Procedure, I invite the representatives of the following countries: Finland, Germany, Italy, Lithuania, Moldova, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, Spain, and Ukraine to participate in this meeting. It is so decided. In accordance with rule 39 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite Ms. Rosemary DiCarlo, Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, to participate in this meeting. It is so decided. In accordance with rule 39 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I also invite His Excellency Mr. Antonio Costa, President of the European Council, to participate in this meeting. It is so decided. The Security Council will now begin its consideration of item 2 of the agenda. I now give the floor to Ms. Rosemary DiCarlo.

Mr. President, we are entering a dangerous new phase in the war in Ukraine. Every day, the attacks are intensifying. Civilian casualties are mounting. The destruction is spreading. The risk of regional spillover is growing. And the consequences are being felt far beyond the battlefield. Make no mistake, this is not simply an escalation in fighting. It is an escalation in human suffering, in regional risk, and in the damage being done to the principles of the UN Charter and the international order. Nowhere is this more painfully evident than in the mounting toll the conflict is taking on civilians in Ukraine. This year has been particularly devastating. In the first eight months alone, more civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine than during the entirety of 2025. The high number of civilian casualties reported so far in September indicates that this deeply troubling trend is continuing. Long-range missile and drone attacks are striking populated areas with increasing frequency, including cities far from the front lines. For weeks, Kyiv and other major cities have endured almost daily attacks, killing and injuring civilians and damaging homes and essential infrastructure. Closer to the front lines, short-range drones and guided aerial bombs continue to exact a devastating toll. At the same time, Repeated attacks on critical civilian infrastructure are making daily life increasingly precarious for millions of Ukrainians. In recent weeks, railway infrastructure, shopping centres, gas stations, warehouses, as well as food and logistics companies have repeatedly been hit. Since February 2022, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights has verified that at least 17,257 civilians, including 835 children, have been killed in Ukraine. A further 53,693 civilians, including 3,247 children, have been injured. The actual figures are likely considerably higher. Mr. President, the civilian impact of the war inside the Russian Federation has also grown significantly over the past year. Russian authorities have reported increasing numbers of civilian casualties from Ukrainian attacks on infrastructure, including commercial warehouses, logistics centers, oil and industrial facilities. Over the weekend, Moscow and other parts of the Russian Federation came under the largest wave of drone attacks to date. From January through August, Russian authorities have reported that 443 civilians were killed and 2,932 injured in the Russian Federation, a sharp increase compared to the same period last year. International humanitarian law is clear. Attacks directed against civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited. These attacks in Ukraine and in the Russian Federation are unacceptable and must stop immediately. Mr. President, concerns continue to grow regarding the fallout of the war in countries neighboring Ukraine and the danger of further expansion. Cross-border drone incursions affecting or approaching the airspace of neighboring states have become increasingly frequent, heightening concerns about the danger of further regional spillover. Attacks on border crossings and transport and logistics infrastructure close to international borders compound these risks. In the past few weeks, alarming incidents involving drones have been reported at Ukraine's border areas with Moldova and Poland, as well as in Lithuania and Romania. Reported military activity in and around Ukraine's nuclear sites, as well as nuclear facilities in the Russian Federation, also remains a grave concern. Any incident that jeopardizes the safety and security of any nuclear facility could have catastrophic consequences. Mr. President, as another wartime winter approaches, Intensifying attacks affecting Ukraine's already strained energy infrastructure are particularly concerning. The cumulative impact of these strikes could plunge millions of people into darkness and cold in the coming months. Everything possible must be done to prevent a further deterioration of the humanitarian situation. We call for urgent steps to end attacks on energy infrastructure and an immediate moratorium on all attacks on population centers. Mr. President, these concerns are compounded by the increasingly dangerous conditions facing humanitarian operations. Between January and July, 10 humanitarian workers were killed and almost 40 injured in Ukraine. At least 19 warehouses have been severely damaged or destroyed, erasing millions of dollars in aid. UN humanitarian convoys have been struck, including during efforts to evacuate civilians. These attacks not only harm individuals, they deprive the most vulnerable of the help they depend on. Furthermore, Civilians in the areas of Ukraine under the temporary occupation of the Russian Federation remain largely beyond our reach due to the persistent lack of access and increasingly dangerous conditions. I urge the sides to ensure safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access to all people in need, wherever they are. Mr. President, the cascading consequences of this war extend far beyond Ukraine, including through growing risks to global food security. Attacks on grain infrastructure, civilian vessels, and ports, together with severe disruption to commercial navigation in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, have impeded agricultural exports from both Ukraine and the Russian Federation. The Food and Agriculture Organization's food price index rose again in August, reaching its highest level since late 2022. The consequences of prolonged disruption will be felt most acutely in import-dependent developing countries already facing high levels of food insecurity. I therefore reiterate the Secretary-General's call on all concerned to ensure freedom of navigation in accordance with international law and to protect civilian ports and maritime infrastructure. The United Nations supports all efforts that can enable food and fertilizer exports to reach world markets safely and predictably. Mr. President, the position of the United Nations regarding Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity is clear and unchanged. The Russian Federation's attempted illegal annexation of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol in 2014, and the attempted illegal annexation of the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia regions of Ukraine in 2022 are invalid and unrecognized by the international community. Under international humanitarian law, the Russian Federation, as an occupying power, is obliged to uphold the laws of Ukraine in force in the territories it occupies. The holding by the Russian Federation of elections to the State Duma this past weekend in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine has no legal grounds. Such actions cannot alter the status of these territories under international law. Mr. President, I reaffirm the United Nations' unwavering commitment to and respect for the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, in line with international law, including the Charter of the United Nations and relevant United Nations resolutions. Nearly five years in, the Russian Federation and Ukraine are facing a stark choice between an even larger conflict and a conscious decision to pursue peace. The choice will impact us all. Ahead of this high-level week, the Secretary-General called on the world leaders to live up to the UN Charter. The full-scale invasion of Ukraine was launched in blatant violation of the Charter and international law. As world leaders gather here in New York, we must reaffirm the principles upon which this organization was founded. We must reaffirm our commitment to the primacy of the peaceful settlement of disputes, and we must reject the use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. We have welcomed various diplomatic efforts to bring this war to an end, including recent renewed engagement by the United States. We hope it will provide an opportunity to re-energize diplomacy and pave the way for the resumption of direct talks. Diplomatic engagement must be matched by meaningful de-escalation. Without it, the dangers to civilians, to the wider region, and to international peace and security will only grow. We therefore reiterate our call to redouble diplomatic efforts towards an immediate, full, and unconditional ceasefire as a first step towards a just, comprehensive, and lasting peace in Ukraine. The United Nations stands ready to support all meaningful efforts to that end. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank Ms. DiCarlo for her briefing. I shall now make a statement in my capacity as the Minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs of France.

Under-Secretary-General, ladies and gentlemen. Almost five years ago, Vladimir Putin threw his own country and his own citizens behind the pursuit of a macabre and paranoia-driven ambition, that of a brutal and illegal aggression against Ukraine. An illegal war, first and foremost, against a sovereign state recognized since 1991 by the international community and by Russia in particular, a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council. A colonial war against a nation whose identity has been called into question, culture denied, history rewritten, and the language defamed by Russia. Let us remember the Mariupol theater and its hundreds of civilian victims. A war that Ukraine did not cause because it was Russia and Russia alone who on the 24th of February 2022 invaded a neighbor that posed no threat to it whatsoever. For Vladimir Putin, this war is a resounding, biting failure. It is the failure of a senseless foray that only one man wanted to see. But who is paying the price for this madness today? It is Ukraine, it is Europe, It is developing countries, the most vulnerable populations throughout the world, and it is the United Nations and its credibility, and it is ultimately Russia itself and its people. Yes, first and foremost, it is Ukraine paying the price. Who can forget the civilian massacres in Bucha in spring of 2022? Since then, the toll has continued to mount. 71,000 civilian victims, including 17,000 deaths since the beginning of the invasion. By targeting strategic infrastructure, electric power stations, nuclear power plants, urban heating grids, drinking water systems, Russia is using winter, the cold, and denial of the most basic needs weapons of mass destruction targeting civilian population. Europe is paying the price. Russia is lashing out at Europe in its entirety through its targeted killings, its acts of sabotage, its cyber attacks, its disinformation, its repeated violation of European airspace. Romania, Poland, Moldova, Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia, Finland, there is not one state who is not now ill at ease as a result of this Russian aggression, which is playing out far from its borders, as we saw yet again recently in Germany, in Leipzig, Germany. neighbor. We stand in full solidarity with you. Who is paying the price of this madness? It is the most vulnerable states and people throughout the world. It is them that are also paying the price for this aggression. Russian attacks are targeting commercial vessels and ports that transport grains and oilseed products from Ukraine in the Black Sea. These are products headed for developing countries. This war is consequently gravely affecting global food Security in its entirety. Through its war of aggression, Russia is striking the very heart of the United Nations. Its Charter is trampled upon by a permanent member of the Security Council who, laughing in the face of the primary responsibility it must uphold, weakens the authority of this organization. What legitimacy can remain for a Security Council of which a permanent member, Russia, increases its human rights violations and its violations of human international humanitarian law, is guilty of abuses classified as war crimes and crimes against humanity by the independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, a permanent member whose leader is the subject of an ICC arrest warrant for the war crime of the deportation and illegal transfer of children. Yes, Vladimir Putin is throwing into disrepute the seat of Russia's seat as a permanent member and is besmirching this council in the eyes of the world. Ladies and gentlemen, who is paying the price for this madness? It is Russia itself. Annihilated, ruined, isolated by this war that only one man wanted. Annihilated. Russia is annihilated. The stubbornness of a man, one man, has already doomed 500,000 Russians to death that had no say in the matter. They have died as a result of a war that is not theirs in a country that is not theirs. Ruined. The Russia of Vladimir Putin is ruined. It is now the Russia of inflation and stagflation. This country is rationing the sale of fuel in the majority of its regions. The civilian economy has been monopolized by the war and is collapsing. There is a public deficit that is two and a half times higher than predicted. And all of this is working to the detriment of basic services that the population require. Isolated, Vladimir Putin's Russia is isolated. It was expelled from the G8 following the illegal annexation of Crimea. Now Russia is isolated, from the Human Rights Council and excluded from the Council of Europe. Russia is isolated in the UN General Assembly. On 10 separate occasions, 10 separate occasions, and with a vast majority, the GA has condemned its aggression, called for a ceasefire, and called for the full respect of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. And yet, another way forward is possible, that of a ceasefire first and foremost. This war has raged for too long. France, once again, called calls for an immediate ceasefire on current front lines because words calling for peace are heard louder when the guns fall silent. For more than a year now, Ukraine has been proposing the principle of an immediate ceasefire. We cannot simply settle for the fact and resign ourselves to the fact that Russia continues to respond through shelling. The very President of the Republic said just this at the rostrum of the General Assembly. France supports the establishment of a double moratorium. That is, on the one hand, attacks on energy and critical civil infrastructure on both sides of the front line, and on the other hand, a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea as a first step in de-escalation. There is, of course, then the path of negotiation. Ukraine is ready for peace. It has expressed the desire for peace and is met only with Moscow's stubbornness. Kyiv has clearly expressed its desire for peace and on several occasions has demonstrated it is ready and willing to engage honestly and candidly in a negotiating process. The Ukrainian president has also said he's ready to meet his Russian counterpart. For as long as Russia fails to commit to negotiations, we will continue to ratchet up our collective pressure on Russia to compel it to negotiate in good faith and to cease its senseless aggression. Ladies and gentlemen, the only solution possible is that of a just, lasting peace in accordance with international law and the United Nations Charter. This solution must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. Vladimir Putin has failed. Ukraine and the international community are paying the price. The Russian people are too. This madness must stop. I thank you. And I now resume my function as Council President.
And I give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Edgars Rinkevics, President of the Republic of Latvia.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. I thank Under-Secretary-General Nikouliou for her briefing. Some countries like to speak about the root causes of this war. But let us be clear. The root cause of this suffering in Ukraine, and now increasingly beyond Ukraine, is Russia's revisionist ambition to overturn the international order. A permanent member of this Council is seeking to bring a sovereign nation to its knees through brute worse. Instead of seeking peace, Russia only escalates. More missiles, more drones, more deaths. It brings destruction while abusing its permanent seat on this very Council, United Nations Security Council. Permanent membership was never intended as a shield for aggression. It comes with a special responsibility, and that special responsibility is to uphold international peace and security. It's not a privilege to violate it. The task of this Council is to stop this war. Latvia continues to call for an immediate ceasefire. Latvia supports every meaningful effort towards a just and lasting peace. We welcome active United States engagement, including the first visit of the Special Envoy to Kyiv. But while others pursue peace, Russia intensifies its attacks. Mr. President, month after month, Russia drives the civilian toll higher. As winter approaches, Latvia calls on every country to help shield Ukraine's people by supporting its air defense and safeguarding the energy system, the system on which millions depend. Unable to conquer Ukraine, Russia seeks to make it unlivable. What military purpose is served by striking apartment buildings where families sleep? What military purpose is served by destroying schools? Or what military purpose is served by striking kindergartens? These are not isolated attacks. They are part of a wider campaign against Ukraine's people, Ukraine's identity, and Ukraine's future. Russia must disclose the whereabouts of thousands of abducted Ukrainian children. And Russia must return them home, because they are children of Ukraine. Russia also must end torture in its detention facilities. Provide the United Nations system and international monitors full and unimpeded access to the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. And finally, Russia must end targeting those trying to help. Attacks on clearly marked UN convoys are indefensible. Russia continues targeting ships and infrastructure that purpose is to feed people around the globe. And Russia must stop this activity as well. Russia must stop trying to break our resolve to support Ukraine. Across Europe, it seeks to do just that through drone incursions, sabotage, arson, and disinformation. Russia will not succeed. And our resolve will not weaken. Mr. President, aggression against a sovereign state cannot be rewarded. The way this war ends will define the world we leave to the next generations. Our collective action is a test of the United Nations and the United Nations Charter itself. Are we ready to sacrifice the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity? Latvia's answer is clear. We stand with Ukraine. We stand for the principles of the United Nations Charter. And we stand for the peace and security. I thank you.
I wish to thank His Excellency Mr. Rinkievich. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Lars Løkke Rasmussen, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Denmark.

Thank you, Mr. President. Let me also thank Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo for her important briefing. Excellencies, just one month ago, I presided over this Council as we marked Ukraine's Independence Day, a solemn yet powerful reminder of the resilience of the Ukrainian people as they marked 35 years of independence from the former Soviet Union, an independence they fight for today. At that time, I once again called for a swift end to Russia's illegal, unprovoked, and unjustified aggression against Ukraine. Ukraine must be free to determine its own future. It has been said many times before, but it bears repeating here today: If Russia stops fighting, the war ends. If Ukraine stops fighting, it will be the very end of Ukraine. And yet, Russia continues its attempt to oppress its independent neighbor. I have personally witnessed the suffering it has caused with my own eyes in Kyiv. I have seen the consequences of attacks on residential buildings, where families should have been safe, attacks on energy infrastructure, leaving civilians without heat and electricity in the harsh winter, and attacks on healthcare facilities, where those already wounded are once again placed in danger. And yet, the human cost has continued to rise. This summer has seen some of the highest levels of civilian casualties since 2022. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, more than 68,000 civilians have been killed or injured. Denmark pays tribute to all those innocent civilians who have lost their lives in this war. Russia's blatant violation of the UN Charter and of the most fundamental principle of international law must simply stop. Excellencies, we are witnessing a dangerous spiral of escalation. The attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified with huge casualties. Civilian infrastructure and energy facilities continue to be targeted, and this is all the more cynical as winter looms on the horizon. Denmark strongly condemns all attacks in violation of international humanitarian law. Those responsible for violation of international law, including the UN Charter and international humanitarian law, must be held accountable. Excellencies, the consequences of this war do not stop at Ukraine's borders. They are felt across the globe. The Black Sea remains vital for Ukraine and for the wider world. Attacks on Ukrainian ports and grain infrastructure have consequences far beyond the battlefield. They threaten trade, livelihoods, and global food supplies, especially in developing countries. The consequences of Russia's aggression have also significantly impacted the European continent. Several neighboring European countries have experienced Russian airspace violation, drone and missile incidents. And most recently, our neighboring country, Germany, attributed a failed hybrid attack at the Leipzig-Halle Airport to Russia. These are reckless and dangerous acts. They form part of a broader pattern of Russian provocations and malign activities designed to disrupt, intimidate, and spread instability across Europe. Europe is not and will not be intimidated. We will strengthen our deterrence and hold Russia accountable. Excellencies, we welcome the recent peace efforts undertaken by the United States, including President Trump's engagement and the latest visits of U.S. envoys to Russia and Ukraine. A peaceful settlement concerning Ukraine cannot be decided without Ukraine. And similarly, Europe must be meaningfully involved, as Ukraine's security is also Europe's security. Ukraine has repeatedly, again and again, demonstrated its readiness to agree to a ceasefire. Russia, by contrast, has ignored these proposals and continued to escalate. Excellencies, Ukraine can count on Denmark's support. We will continue to provide financial and security assistance as Ukraine defends itself against Russia's aggression. We will help Ukraine rebuild. We will provide lifesaving humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, including through our contributions to the UN. And we will increase the pressure on Russia through tough EU sanctions. Excellencies, in closing, there is absolutely no alternative to a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace based on international law, including the principles of the UN Charter. We once again demand that Russia urgently and immediately accepts an immediate and unconditional ceasefire. That it finally decides to live with its neighbors in peace, respecting their independence, their borders and the right to freely determine their own future. Denmark will continue to stand by Ukraine. We will strive for a Europe and a world in which peace is based not on the power to conquer, are on the power of law. Thank you.

I thank His Excellency Mr. Rasmussen for that statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Ed Miliband, Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs of the United Kingdom.

Thank you. Let me thank Under-Secretary-General de Carle for her briefing. Let me say clearly to begin with that Foreign Minister Sabir, Andriy The United Kingdom stands with Ukraine and its people, and we stand with you as long as it takes. And more than four and a half years since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, we must be under no illusion. We are at this point because of Russia's deliberate choices. Russia chose an illegal and unprovoked invasion. Russia chooses to escalate its war. And Russia chooses to reject efforts towards peace. And we should all be under no illusions about what is at stake. Because Russia's attack is not just an attack on Ukraine. It is an attack on the, it is an assault on the core principles of the UN Charter. It is an assault on us all. Sham elections in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory are just the latest demonstration of this. A blatant violation of Ukraine's sovereignty. For all our sakes, we cannot accept the changing of borders by force, and we cannot accept a world in which sovereignty can be trampled by aggressors. As others have said, no nation in this Chamber is insulated from the consequences of this war. Russia's war hurts our populations at home. Russian strikes on Black Sea ports and merchant shipping threaten global food supplies. Russia as my Danish colleague said, continues to pursue reckless hybrid activity, most recently the outrageous attack at Leipzig airport. Let me be very clear. The United Kingdom, Europe and NATO do not seek conflict with Russia. NATO is and always will be a defensive alliance. But we will continue to call out and act against Russia's hostile activity, whatever form it takes. That applies to Russian aggression against Ukraine just as strongly as it does to Russia's unacceptable and intensifying hybrid threats across Europe. President, Russia could choose a different course today. agree a ceasefire, come to the negotiating table and begin rebuilding a relationship based on sovereignty, international law and the UN Charter. But that is not Russia's chosen path. This summer, Russia launched record numbers of ballistic missiles and drones against Ukrainian cities. Civilian casualties have tragically risen to the highest levels since 2022. We meet as Ukrainian civilians, and I think we should think of them today, brace for another hard, unbearable winter. Another winter of anxiety under attack from missiles and drones. Another winter when Russia will target energy and infrastructure to plunge Ukraine into cold and darkness. Russia's own defence ministry has spoken of making Ukraine, and I quote, "freeze". That tells us all we need to know about its intentions. Here at the UN, of all places, we cannot just shrug and normalise these barbarous and illegal tactics. Ukraine has repeatedly called for peace, offering a ceasefire and engaging constructively with US-led efforts. The principles for a credible negotiation remain clear: a full and unconditional ceasefire, respect for Ukraine's sovereignty, robust security arrangements. President, we will back Ukraine through the coming winter and beyond. We will increase economic pressure on Russia. and we will support serious diplomacy to reach a just and lasting peace. In closing, I want to address the Russian representative directly, because the foreign minister will be speaking later. I know from my family history what it looks like when war ravages Europe. My parents saw it as refugees from Poland and Belgium in the Second World War. We lost countless family members. Today, war has returned to Europe, the worst conflict since that time. Innocent civilians losing their lives. And why? Because Russia chose to launch this unjustified, unprovoked, and illegal conflict. And even if morality does not sway the Russian Government, reality should. We all know that Russia is failing in this war. Four years ago, Putin sought to erase Ukraine's independence, but Ukraine's national resolve has proved to be unwavering. Four years ago, Putin expected Ukraine's supporters to fold, but our backing is rock solid. Four years ago, Putin believed time would favour Russia, yet Russia's advances have all but stalled, and the number of Russian military personnel killed or wounded has passed 1.5 million. And on top of that, Russia's economy is ailing as the consequences of Putin's choices mount, and sanctions deprive the Kremlin war machine of revenues. I say to the Russian representative, it is time ministers told President Putin the truth. The world knows that Russia is failing in this war. The Russian people can feel it. And ministers know it too. They should tell President Putin to end the bloodshed. And let me tell this truth. The UK's commitment will not waver. Our allies' commitment will not waver. We stand with Ukraine now. We will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes.
I thank His Excellency, Mr. Miliband, for that statement. And I now give the floor to His Excellency, Rivia Martinez Acha Vasquez, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Panama.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Panama thanks the Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, Ms. Rosemary DiCarlo, for her invaluable briefing. We also welcome the distinguished authorities that accompany us today in this Chamber to once again broach the situation in Ukraine. Once again, We wish to say that the passage of time cannot turn a tragedy into a diplomatic routine. The war continues to rage on. Civilians continue to die. Cities continue to be attacked. And peace continues to remain elusive. Panama cannot settle for or get used to war. Neither can the United Nations. Mr. President. For almost two years, Panama has had the honor and the responsibility of serving as an elected member on this Security Council. From this seat, we have defended a conviction that does not change with circumstances or alliances. The United Nations Charter is not a declaration of good intentions; it is the legal foundation of the international order. It provides for the use of force and states that as a principle, sovereignty, political independence, and the territorial integrity of states are its principles, as are the need to resolve disputes by peaceful means. These are not optional principles. These are the rules that we have set ourselves to avoid force, strength, might from replacing law. And if we allow these rules to be eroded in different contexts, for example, in wars as a result of geopolitical situations or in line with the agendas of the strongest, we will not only be weakening Ukraine, but weakening the very system which protects all states, large and small. Mr. President, the war has taken on a particularly alarming dimension. Missiles and drones are reaching populated areas. energy and civilian infrastructure continue under pressure. Ports and maritime waterways are under increasing risk. Behind every figure there is a person, a parent, a father, a mother, a child, a family. The civilian population in Ukraine and Russia cannot become the price of war. International humanitarian law is clear and unflinching. Citizens must be protected. Civilian infrastructure cannot become a target, and all parties, without exception, must uphold their obligations under international humanitarian law. There are no political circumstances which mean that one is exempt from these obligations. There is no military target that can justify the abandonment of humankind, and there is no military victory that can erode suffering of a population or make it justifiable. We also note with grave concern the risk of the conflict expanding. Each new front, each new escalation, each attack that transcends borders increases the risk of a regional conflagration. Escalation does not bring us any closer to peace. It dims the prospect of negotiations. Consequently, we must have the political courage to say what is plain before our eyes. This war will not have a lasting solution found on the battlefield. field, it will have to finish at a negotiating table. And the earlier we arrive at that negotiating table, the fewer lives we will lose. I agree with exactly what the UK Foreign Minister said. We're talking here about avoiding the loss of human life. Panama makes a clear appeal. An immediate, verifiable ceasefire respected by all parties is what we need. We need a ceasefire that must not become, and does not become, a simple pause between offensive. It must be the beginning of a serious political process. We need real negotiations that are direct and conducted in good faith, supported by verification mechanisms and designed to resolve substantive issues that have caused this conflict to drag out. Diplomacy cannot be used as a facade, a veneer, while weapons continue to talk. Negotiating does not mean turning our back on principles. Negotiating means finding a us forward to preserve our principles through peace. Consequently, we support all genuine diplomatic efforts that might bring about a cessation of hostilities and a just, lasting and sustainable peace, which is fully in line with the United Nations Charter and international law. Mr. President, the transnational nature of this war cannot be ignored either. What is happening in the Black Sea does not finish at its coasts. When Commercial navigation is under threat when we attack ports and civilian vessels, and when we disrupt agricultural exports, the consequences reach markets, homes, and communities far beyond Europe. Maritime security and food security are inextricably linked for a country such as Panama, whose prosperity and safety are inextricably linked with freedom of navigation and the respect for international law of the sea. These are not abstract concepts, therefore, for us. They are essential principles for stability and prosperity of the world at large. Excellencies, Panama wishes to voice its concern at the recruitment of Panamanian citizens and citizens of other countries to participate in this conflict, including nationals, particularly from Latin America. Every foreign national recruited to fight on the front lines is 1 more life exposed to a war which continues to take on international dimensions. We must pay greater attention to this phenomenon and step up efforts to prevent people from third countries joining the ranks in a war that has already produced an unconscionable human cost. Today, I wish to issue a very specific humanitarian appeal to both parties. To the Russian Federation and Ukraine, Panama wishes to ask you respectfully to use mechanisms and competent authorities to facilitate the return to Panama of Panamanian citizens who, by any means, might have come to join and participate in this conflict, but who wish to return to their homeland. I must recognise the timely movements by the Ukrainian Government that have allowed these citizens to be repatriated. We have full respect for the sovereignty of both States for their internal affairs and the decisions taken by their and authorities, but for Panama, each citizen counts. No Panamanian person must be forgotten in a war that is not his or her own. I wish to sincerely thank Ukraine for the consideration it has shown to this request and the fact that it has heeded it. I thank it for our bilateral contacts, which have seen us work for the return of Panamanian citizens. We deeply value that humanitarian gesture, and we hope that very soon indeed we will also be able to thank the Russian consideration, following a similar gesture, one that might allow our compatriots who wish to do so to return to Panama. Distinguished Excellencies present, after almost five years of war, we must ask ourselves what message this council is sending out to the world. Are we suggesting that might can replace right, that borders can be redrawn through with the use of weapons? Are we saying that the civilian population can indefinitely endure the consequences of military decisions? Or Or are we saying that even in the darkest times, the international community continues to believe in diplomacy, the Charter and peace? Panama knows what our answer must be. We must always choose peace, but a genuine peace. A genuine peace is not simply the absence of gunfire. Peace is the result of respect for law. Peace is the protection of civilians. Peace is the security of states. Peace is the freedom of navigation. Peace is the possibility for future generations to live free of fear. Consequently, Panama today reiterates its appeal for an immediate and verifiable ceasefire, for the full respect of international humanitarian law, and for the opening of serious, credible and good-faith negotiations able to bring us to a permanent political solution. President, history will judge our decisions, not simply in light of the resolutions we adopt, but in light of the lives that we're able to protect. We'll not be judged only by the words that we state, but rather by our ability to turn them into diplomatic gestures. And we'll not be judged only by how we defend the Charter when it's convenient to do so, but by our resolve to defend it when it's most difficult to do so. Panama states the following in the most lucid terms: "War cannot become the new normal. Might, strength, force cannot replace law, and peace cannot continue to be a promise delayed. The time for the guns to fall silent has come. The time has come to sit at the negotiating table. The time has come to use diplomacy and allow it to speak more strongly than weapons. Because if the United Nations Charter was born to avoid the world once again falling in the abyss of war, our responsibility today is to guarantee that this abyss does not once again become our destiny. Thank you.
I thank His Excellency, Mr. Achavazquez, for his declaration. And I now give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Abdullah T. Bin Rashi Al Zayed, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Bahrain.
