The parties concerned and the broader international community should join hands to strive for a dawn of peace the soonest and promote a political settlement of the crisis. First, the parties to the conflict must exercise restraint and end the hostilities as soon as possible. Since the beginning of this year, the parties have engaged in successive rounds of intense confrontation. As more advanced weaponry continues to be deployed to the battlefield, fighting on the ground risk escalating and expanding, resulting in heavy civilian casualties and serious damage to civilian infrastructure, including energy, agriculture, and logistics facilities. The humanitarian situation is concerning. China calls on the parties to remain calm and exercise restraint, strictly abide by international humanitarian law, refrain from attacking civilians, civilian infrastructure, and humanitarian workers, and make every effort to de-escalate the situation and foster hope for peace. Second, the parties must work toward the same goal and persist in advancing the peace process. Dialogue and negotiation offer the only viable path to resolving the Ukraine crisis. Recently, there has been a series of engagements and interactions among key stakeholders. China welcomes these developments. The negotiating table is the starting point for peace. Despite the current gaps in positions, as long as the dialogues continue, it will be possible to find a solution and open the door to peace. China supports the parties in seeking common ground while shelving their differences and building consensus through negotiation with a view to reaching a comprehensive, lasting and binding peace agreement. Third, it is vital to adopt a long-term perspective and strive to build common security. The current state of the Ukraine situation is due to a complex historical context and contemporary factors. This crisis shows us that no country in the world can enjoy so-called "absolute security." Taking seriously each other's security concerns and building relations of harmony and friendship is the only realistic choice. China calls on all parties concerned to abandon Cold War mentalities and bloc confrontation. embrace a vision of common, comprehensive, cooperative, and sustainable security, finding the greatest common denominator that addresses the concerns of all sides, and build a balanced, effective, and sustainable regional security architecture. China's position on the Ukraine issue has been consistent and crystal clear. We remain guided by the four shoulds proposed by President Xi Jinping, namely: The sovereignty and territorial integrity of all countries should be respected, the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations should be observed, the legitimate security concerns of all countries should be taken seriously, and all efforts conducive to a peaceful solution should be supported. China did not create the Ukraine crisis, and nor is it a party to the conflict. We act only in ways that contribute to peace, and have worked relentlessly to promote peace talks. For over four years, China has maintained close communications with Russia, Ukraine, and other relevant parties. China's special envoy has been conducting shuttle diplomacy. Together with Brazil and other countries of the Global South, China has launched the Friends of Peace Group, continuously garnering consensus and advancing peace efforts. We remain committed to working with the international community and playing a constructive role in the political settlement of the crisis. Thank you, President.
I thank the Permanent Representative of China for his statement. I give the floor to the Permanent Representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. President. Pakistan welcomes the high-level participation in this meeting. And let me also join colleagues in thanking Under-Secretary-General Rosemary DiCarlo for her briefing. President, regrettably, this conflict has raged on for over four years now. It has deeply impacted the regional as well as international security paradigm. Equally concerning have been its repercussions on the global food and energy security, felt far beyond the confines of its geographic scope, disproportionately impacting the developing countries in particular. Of late, the sharp escalation in attacks from both sides involving modern weaponry is deplorable and disturbing. Pakistan delegation has consistently expressed concerns on the humanitarian consequences of this conflict. We once again call upon both parties to desist from further expanding the conflict, to take measures to de-escalate, scrupulously abide by international law and international humanitarian law obligations, and recommit to dialogue. to bring an early end to this conflict. President, it is more than evident that there is no military solution to this conflict. And every minute, hour, and day spent in fighting is taking the parties further apart, making the path to peace more While accomplishing a just and lasting peace and bringing this conflict to an end has proved quite onerous, this effort must not be abandoned merely because there are challenges to be confronted. A year and a half ago, this Council adopted the US-sponsored resolution 2774, imploring a swift end to this conflict. Pakistan supported that resolution. Since that time, the United States has led the efforts to give effect to the call for peace made in that resolution. And we also heard President Trump yesterday about the continuing push for peace. We commend these efforts and hope that they will succeed. This will be possible if the parties concerned earnestly commit to dialogue, demonstrate necessary political will, and continue to meaningfully engage in this process to secure lasting peace in the region, and more importantly, for those directly affected by this conflict. Let me restate, even at the risk of repetition, our collective priority must be to silence the guns and create conditions for a negotiated settlement. An immediate and comprehensive ceasefire can help the parties bridge differences and move in the direction of peace, which remains the only viable and responsible choice. Pakistan supports all efforts that can help deliver a peaceful resolution of this conflict, which addresses the legitimate security concerns of all sides which is anchored in the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and international law and relevant multilateral agreements. I thank you.

I thank the Permanent Representative of Pakistan.

I now give the floor to the Permanent Representative of the US.

Thank you, Mr. President, for convening this meeting, and thank you, Under-Secretary-General DeCarlo, for your briefing. Colleagues, yesterday, Just a few rooms from here, President Trump stood before the world, stood before the General Assembly, and said again what he has said for the last four years, that killing has to stop. It's important what you did not hear him say. He did not say one side has to win, another side has to win. It's not about winning. All sides are losing. All sides are losing colleagues. The world is losing 25,000 lost souls per month at this point, obviously 25,000 too many, but every month that goes on another 25,000, another 25,000. And while so many In this room and so many forums around the world, in Europe and other places, colleagues, we could fill these rooms with speeches about peace. The president is doing everything he can to actually broker that peace. In this conflict and some of the other forgotten, complicated, or far-flung conflicts. And as he said yesterday, he is fully committed to facilitating peace in this war. Over the last 4 and 1/2 years, young men have been fed into trenches and killing fields by the tens of thousands. Families have buried sons, fathers, wives, sisters, children, apartment buildings, hospitals, schools, ports, power have been destroyed and are being destroyed right now as we speak. And this war is spreading beyond the battlefield. Missiles and drone attacks threaten commercial shipping, Black Sea food grain exports, and are now threatening the world's poorest families with famine. Strikes on energy infrastructure are raising costs far beyond Russia and Ukraine and into Africa, into Asia, and into the rest of the world. The President has been clear since day one that the war has to stop. We should note that the rhetoric in this Council and elsewhere have shifted to ending the war, which is a positive thing. But now we have violations of neighboring airspace, including NATO airspace, that create risks that no one in this room takes lightly. And I want to be clear that we condemn in the strongest terms any attempts to broaden the war. And we also condemn any attack that threatens the free flow of food into global markets. And we join my colleague from Colombia, my colleagues from Panama and others. And we should talk about more. We should continue to talk about the recruiting of our nationals around the world as mercenaries, as fighters, whatever label you want to put on it. We should include in that the recruiting of a Cuban mercenaries. that are now being pulled into this war with full knowledge of the Cuban regime. So again, the spreading of this conflict is unacceptable. It is dangerous. And I appreciate many of the remarks and speeches today in supporting our efforts. Hasn't always been that way, frankly, but in supporting our efforts to try to end this war before it spreads out of control. Colleagues, roughly a third of the world's wheat supply stands in the balance now, as does the risk of famine for millions of the world's most vulnerable should these disruptions continue. So again, the message from President Trump is this, don't widen the war. recognize that there is no military solution to this war, and return to the negotiating table. And there are areas of common ground, and particularly in energy security and food security, where we do think there could be some reasonable incremental steps towards peace. But, colleagues, we have to make the way for peace. Special envoys, Witkoff and Kushner, have been carrying that message directly to Kyiv, directly to Moscow, They have worked tirelessly at great personal cost and out of love for country and love for peace. And the United States is prepared to mediate, to facilitate trilateral talks, to use every diplomatic opening available to bring the parties together. And we welcome other efforts. We welcome efforts from India, from Turkey, and from others to bring peace. And we And our inexhaustible special envoys will keep showing up. We will keep talking. We will keep giving diplomacy a chance. And we will keep working until there is a path to a ceasefire, an end to the war, and a negotiated settlement. We know this is where this war has to land and how it has to end. And just let me say this. As the president charges forward to bring peace between these countries, let's take a moment and admire the example of First Lady Melania Trump, who has worked with both Russia and Ukraine to secure the return of children separated from their families by this war. And I know you will agree with me that it is children who painfully suffer in any of these conflicts, and particularly this one, and her work is a reminder That even in the middle of a brutal war, when everything seems intractable, the two sides can do something which, again, not too long ago was was thought unthinkable. If she can set that example, I think there is hope and there is a path. Both sides can still talk and these children can come home. And if Russia and Ukraine can work to reunite children with their families. then they can sit across the table and begin the much harder work of ending this conflict. Peace will require difficult choices from all sides. It will require compromise. It will require leaders to recognize that another 25,000 lives just by the time we talk about this again, it's completely, it's just completely unacceptable. President Trump and the United States government are doing our part We hope and pray Russia and Ukraine will do theirs. Please, colleagues, let's stop the killing and let's make way for peace. And I thank you.
I thank the representative of the United States of America for his statement. And I give the floor to His Excellency, Mr. Andriy Sybiya, Minister for Foreign Affairs of Ukraine.

Mr. President, members of the Council, distinguished heads of state, colleagues, This is the fifth General Assembly session since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the 13th since Putin began this war. This is the longest, most devastating, most dangerous war in Europe since the Second World War. So many speeches have been made in this Council, so many right words, but the war drags on. I don't want to make another speech that will not stop the war. Enough speeches, enough broken promises, enough imitation of diplomacy, enough. This war has to stop. Ukraine wants to end it now, not later. And we are ready for a full, unconditional ceasefire, ready for ceasefires on energy and food, ready to stop right now, right here. And we were not the ones who started it. We were invaded. We keep on fighting, defending our home. I'll tell you more. There are 15 members of this council. 14 support in one way or another an immediate ceasefire, including four permanent members, including the United States and China. Only one state blocks an end to hostilities, and it is the aggressor itself. Russia vetoes not just a ceasefire. Russia vetoes peace. Putin could have ended this war long ago, but he chooses daily escalation. And I want to make it clear, if we don't force Russia to accept ceasefire now, ahead of us will be even more escalation caused by Russia. The Council was built on the ashes of the most devastating war in human history. Its foundation stands on 80 million graves. Have we forgotten? It was created to make the Second World War also the last world war. But today we are closer than ever to another global catastrophe, because Putin does not abandon his plan to destroy Ukraine at any cost. This is not a Ukrainian war, not even a European one. It is a global threat. Preventing the worst scenario depends on everyone in this room and beyond it. Colleagues, no one needs another speech that does not stop the war. Instead, let's ask questions that lead to action. First, Why this war matters to everyone. Second, why it cannot be normalized. And third, why it cannot be stopped by appeasement. First, anyone who says this is not our war is wrong. This is everyone's war because its consequences reach everywhere. When Russia first blocked Ukrainian ports four years ago, food prices jumped 25% worldwide. Africa, Asia, and the Middle East were hit hardest. Right now, because Putin refuses to end this war, the Black Sea is blocked again. 400 million people who depend on Ukrainian grain are not getting it. 11 million tons risk spoiling. The damage will last many years if we don't restore freedom of navigation now. Across Africa, Russia recruits young men into its army by promising fake job and scholarship offers. We have identified at least 3,000 mercenaries from 37 African countries in the Russian army. And those are only the documented cases. Encouraged by his staged elections, Putin now plans a new draft at home and even more aggressive recruitment across Africa, the Middle East, Asia, and Latin America. In the Middle East, Iran and its friends, Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis, grow bolder by the day. Moscow backs Tehran with weapons, technology, and intelligence. Chaos and high oil prices in the region are favorable for Russia and its war budget. In Asia, Russia is dragging North Korea directly into this war, destabilizing the Korean Peninsula. 20,000 troops already deployed, many more thousands this year if Putin does not stop. In return, Kim gets technology, training, resources, such as Russian-trained drone operators. There are no guarantees that he will not use them to destabilize the Korean Peninsula and the entire Indo-Pacific. In Central Asia and South Caucasus, Russia uses economic pressure and energy blackmail to destabilize its neighbors, recruiting their citizens and exposing their economies to secondary sanctions. In Latin America, this war means Russia's intensified predatory recruitment and state propaganda dividing societies. Even in Europe, some politicians still say, "This is not our war." They must be blind. Russia already wages war on Europe. Arson, assassination, cyber attacks, disinformation, election meddling, the weaponization of energy, food, and migration, drones, and missiles crossing into NATO airspace. This is not hybrid. Drop this word. Russia's war against Europe is no longer hybrid. Instead of safeguarding peace, Russia is spreading war. That is everyone's problem. Second, this war cannot be normalized. Getting used to horrifying headlines does not make them less tragic. The world must not get used to this war. Take one town, Oleshky, and its wider community on the occupied left bank of Dnipro. Under siege, food, meds, electricity, gas, all cut off. As winter approaches, Russia is deliberately making life there impossible. They are starving them to death. No country, no international organization can reach those people. Every day, they run out of food, out of water, and all resources to live. The world rightly condemned the siege of Leningrad by Nazis. Today, Russia applies the same method against Ukrainians. The Kremlin reproduces the crimes of the past. And this policy echoes an older wound, the Holodomor genocide, when millions of Ukrainians were deliberately starved by the Kremlin regime. Hunger was Moscow's weapon then, and it's Moscow's weapon now. One Oleshky resident named Alla survives only on tea with honey. The last food delivery reached her town before summer. This is not neglect. OVC monitors call it an engineered blockade. Russia does not let people live because it uses them as human shields. If you remember one thing from this meeting, remember Oleshky. Hear their cry for help. Demand Russia open humanitarian corridors. Moscow is the only cause of this disaster and the only obstacle to ending it. Oleshky is only one horror among many. In the first half of this year, more Ukrainian civilians were killed than in any same period in four years. And each month has broken this sad record. Russian forces have committed nearly 900 documented acts of sexual violence against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners. 16 of these victims were children, some as young as four. This cannot be normalized. Third, this war cannot be stopped by appeasement. This is not the United Nations Impunity Council. even though Russia wishes it to be. And let me remind, Russia occupies the seat of the Soviet Union illegally. The aggressor must be removed from this table. The mission of this Council is to safeguard peace and security. If Russia vetoes peace, we must veto Russia's war. That means concrete steps. Intensify diplomacy to end this war. Demand Russia accept a ceasefire. Cut off the resources fueling its terror. Strengthen sanctions. End Russia's access to technology. Expose its recruitment, disinformation, and destabilization. Provide Ukraine with what we need to defend our people in winter. Help us bring home our abducted children. Join our fight for accountability. Every country that refuses to support Russia's war can contribute to peace. Act now. Russia is never as strong as it wants us to believe, and never as weak as we want it to be. Russia is no longer a global power. It is a global problem, and it requires a global solution. Mr. President, the Russian representative, the Russian minister spoke, sits at this table. I made an effort. I made an effort to listen to his boring fairy tales and manipulations to make sure they haven't changed. One phrase said it all. We are, I'm citing him, we are not going to stop our special military operation. He offered many reasons why Russia continues this war. He blamed Ukraine, the United States, the West, NATO, anyone but Putin. He tried to present -- even tried to present Russia as the victim. But instead, listen carefully to what he did not say. I know at least three questions he cannot answer. First, why won't your president sit down with our president to end this war? Second, in August, you lost tens of thousands of soldiers to seize a few square kilometers. What did they die for? And third, you wanted Kyiv in three days. How did you end up with Moscow burning four years later? Silence will be his only honest answer. We must stop this war now, before Putin enters your home. He is already at the entrance. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Cibia for his statement. And I give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Aleksander Stubb, President of the Republic of Finland.

Thank you very much, Mr. President.

Ministers, ambassadors, ladies and gentlemen, I think I sit here today pretty much with three hats. The first one is a Nordic hat. I'm speaking here on behalf of my four Nordic neighbors. The second one is the hat of the President of Finland, who shares a 1,340 kilometer border with Russia. And the third hat I have is as a friend of the United Nations and an admirer of the UN Security Council as a problem solver. And today I have three very simple messages. One is a call to the Security Council to act. The second one is reasons to end this war. And the third one is a few solutions on how one could do that. I tried to be as pragmatic as a Finn can be and as constructive as a friend of Ukraine can be in a very difficult situation. So the first one is a call for the Security Council to act. I've had the chance to listen to many of your interventions here in between. And I think we all share the basic tenets that Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine is a blatant violation of the UN Charter. We also agree that the use of force or the destruction of sovereign equality or the destruction of territorial integrity is a fundamental break of the rules that underpin our whole international system. We see Russia violating these rules every day. We see methods as illegal as the war itself. And, you know, I was struck by Ambassador Walls highlighting some of the key elements of how Russia is systematically targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure. And having visited Ukraine six times in the past three years, I've been there, seen and witnessed what it looks like on the ground. And as a child of the post-Cold War era, I never thought I would see anything like it. But it is a reality and a reality that I think this Council and the United Nations need to fail. We also see a lot of the humanitarian operations under attack, including aid workers being killed. Of course, the aim then is to instill fear and wear down Ukraine. But I would really like to see the Security Council taking more firm action to try to end it. And here's where I come to my second point, the reasons for ending the war. The first one is the most self-evident, and that's what President Trump said yesterday in his speech, and that is, quote, "The killing has to stop." And I think that's a cliche or none for anyone who works for the United Nations or is a member of this assembly. Now, the war is very much a stalemate. This year, Russia has acquired roughly 900 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory, but Ukraine has acquired roughly 800 square kilometers back. So the line of contact is basically not moving. If the aim is to acquire Donbass, at this rate, it will take years. And at this rate, as Ambassador Walsh said, in the Meanwhile, we're killing roughly 25,000 soldiers per month. Put that into perspective, the Soviet war in Afghanistan, 10 years and 18,000 casualties and dead. So we're talking, you know, a number of people dying, which is now going over 1 million. And that in my mind is a waste of life. So the continuation of this war is a lose-lose. Someone said in their intervention that there is not a military solution to this. I agree. There's no way in which one side or the other is going to exhaust each other. The very simple reason is that we're now seeing a type of modern warfare conducted that is so effective that it cannot end. We haven't seen anything like this previously because we're seeing unmanned vehicles, we're seeing death zones of roughly 20 kilometers to which you cannot enter because with a 95% certainty, you're going to be wiped out. So someone needs to tell, obviously, the aggressor that this is not going to have a military solution. Now, my then final and third point is obviously a call for peace. I mean, I'm sure everyone in this room wants peace. And we have to ask the question, how do we do it? That's what the Americans have been trying to do now actively for about a year and a half. And of course, the starting point is very simple. If we lived in an ideal world, we would first have an unconditional ceasefire, which Foreign Minister Zbigniew was referring to, or even a conditional ceasefire, which is linked to energy or to grain, because we all understand that this is not a regional war. It's a regional war with global ramifications on food prices and on energy prices. The second part is the beginning of peace negotiations. I think we've had enough wars to understand that peace negotiations usually last a long time, but there has to become a time when the killing stops, and then we start negotiating about security, about territory, about permanent solutions, and also about justice. So I'd like to finish by thanking all of those countries who are involved in this peace mediation, the United States primarily, but also countries such as India, Turkey, or the Arab Emirates who've been active lately on some of the more specific issues. And I would also like to thank leaders such as Prime Minister Modi or President Erdogan or President Tokayev, who have publicly called for this war to end, as has President Xi. So I think at the end of the day, you know, this is my third time speaking in this room in my capacity as president of Finland about the war. And I think I speak, I know I speak on behalf of all the Nordics when I say that it would be very good if the President of Finland did not have to come here next year to give the same speech about ending this war. And I think it's the duty and it's the job of this Security Council to end it. So I hope we can all double down our efforts towards a just and lasting peace. And just to quote late President Martti Ahtisaari and Nobel Peace Laureate, he once said that what humans began, they can also end. So please, Russia, end this war.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Stoob for his statement, and I give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Nicolae Dancil, President of Romania.

Mr. President. Distinguished members of the Council, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine reached a critical juncture. We agree on the need to achieve a just and lasting peace in Ukraine and to restore compliance with the United Nations Charter, as does the overwhelming majority of this Council and United Nations members. I come before the Council with a message of responsibility and solidarity. Romania is firmly committed to the United Nations Charter and to the principle of sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, which apply to all nations. These principles have been profoundly shaken by the Russian Federation's war of aggression against Ukraine. A few months ago, A Russian drone crashed at night into a residential building in the city of Galati in Romania, recklessly endangering the lives of innocent Romanian civilians. Russian drones breach our national airspace with increasing frequency and in disregard of international law. This violation now extends into the maritime domain, to our exclusive economic zone on 20th of August, a Russian Navy drone came dangerously close to the Neptune Deep offshore gas installation in the Black Sea. Developments in the Black Sea, a region vital to global security and prosperity and strategic bridge between Asia, Europe, Middle East and Africa, caused serious disruption to global food supply chains and lead to growing maritime insecurity. We have brought this risk to the attention of the Council on numerous occasions. Infringement of freedom of navigation have become recurrent, including intensified strikes on Ukraine ports and on commercial shipping on the Danube and in the Black Sea. They disregard provisions of the United Nations Convention on the Law on the Sea and endanger the safety and security of seafarers from around the world, among them, nation of member states of this Council. The massive and repeated bombardment of Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities is unacceptable. Deliberate attacks against the civilian population and critical infrastructure amount to war crimes. Full responsibility for such violations and their consequences rests with the perpetrators. The international law is clear. Ukraine has a legitimate right to self-defense under Article 51 of the United Nations Charter. In defending itself, Ukraine upholds the principle that is fundamental for all of us, the right of every state to freely choose its future. That is why our solidarity with Ukraine and our resolve in addressing the regional and global consequences of the war remain unwavering. As Ukraine's western neighbor with the longest common border, Romania has continuously facilitated the access of Ukrainian grains to consumers around the world and has provided shelter to Ukrainians who sought refuge in our country or transited through it. Together with Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova and the European Union, we continue to work to increase the transit of Ukrainian grain through the Danube and the Romanian port of Constanca. Through the EU solidarity lanes, we help keep grain and food available and affordable for countries across the Middle East and Africa. So we call for restoring the freedom of navigation in the Black Sea, which is crucial for global security and prosperity. We have made significant progress in establishing the EU Maritime Security Hub in the Black Sea to strengthen situational awareness and coordination. Together with Bulgaria and Turkey, we have deepened our regional partnership from demining to the protection of key maritime infrastructure. So partners around the world can count on Romania. The time has come for peace in Ukraine. The longer the conflict continues, the greater the risk that it spread beyond Ukraine borders and threaten security and stability across the region. We urge an immediate cessation of the Russian war against Ukraine. We call on Russia to choose diplomacy over escalation and to change course towards peace. President Zelensky and Ukraine had repeatedly expressed their readiness for meaningful, good-faith negotiations. We support a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in line with international law and the United Nations Charter, and in full observance of the principle of sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity within internationally recognized borders, with robust and credible security guarantees for Ukraine. We appreciate the renewed efforts of Ukraine, the United States, and European partners, and we expect the Russian Federation to respond to the call for an immediate, full, and unconditional ceasefire. President Trump's commitment in bringing this war to a close reflects exactly the kind of strength, leadership, and strategic clarity needed to preserve peace and stability in Europe. The Romanian people deeply appreciate his resolve to pursue conditions that can support a lasting and just peace, and I would like to thank him publicly for these efforts today. Romania will do its part, will support credible efforts grounded in the United Nations Charter and international law, aimed at securing peace, strengthening stability, and restoring the security architecture undermined by this war. As a neighbor and as a friend, Romania will continue to stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes. Thank you.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Dan for that statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Peter Pellegrini, President of the Slovakian Republic.

Thank you very much, Excellencies. I would like to thank France for organising the Security Council meeting and for the opportunity to address this session. When we met here last year, we marked 80 years since the founding of the United Nations. It was a moment built on a simple promise about how nations should treat one another. And for Slovakia, our commitment to that promise has not changed. We continue to support the basic rules that bring us together every year, that every country has the right to govern itself, that borders must never be changed by force, and that no nation is above the law. Since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, we have supported the Ukrainian people as any responsible neighbor would do. Today, I have two simple messages to offer, both of them equally urgent. First, the deliberate attacks against civilians must stop immediately. And second, diplomacy is the only responsible way to resolve this crisis. prevent further escalation, and create conditions for political settlement that can last. Most of the attacks have nothing to do with military goals anymore. They continue to bring suffering and destruction. Ballistic missiles and drones target homes and civilians, infrastructure, in residential areas of Ukraine day after day. What makes them targets? Nothing. The only goal is to spread terror and paralyze. This is most obvious when we look at the attacks on critical infrastructure. Strikes on energy facilities have triggered electricity supply disruptions again and again. Especially in winter, they turn freezing weather into a weapon against civilians. This is completely unacceptable. As we have said so many times before, there is no military solution to this war. Slovakia has always supported every serious peace effort. We have advocated for a solution that would enhance the overall security and stability of Ukraine and the whole of Europe. After 20 years, Slovakia is ready to serve this body once again as a non-permanent member. We are prepared to be a responsible partner offering a balanced approach, ready to contribute to any meaningful path towards peace, because stepping up diplomacy is our only option. The upcoming winter will be critical for Ukraine. However, there is still no de-escalation in sight. Slovakia strongly supports a ceasefire to protect innocent civilians from bitter winter conditions. That is why we welcome the most recent mediation talks led by the United States. They deserve support from partners in Europe to help bring Ukraine and Russia to the negotiating table. Even a partial ceasefire could lead to a broader agreement later. It would be a clear signal that there is a serious will to stop senseless atrocities and achieve a lasting peace in line with the UN Charter. Thank you very much.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Pellegrini for that statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Rob Jetten, Prime Minister and Minister for General Affairs of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Mr. President. And I have the honour to speak on behalf of the Benelux countries, Belgium, Luxembourg, and my own country, the Kingdom of the Netherlands. After more than four and a half years of Russia's full-scale war of aggression, our message remains unchanged. Russia's aggression is not only an attack on Ukraine, but on the principles of the UN Charter. Borders cannot be changed by force and aggression cannot be rewarded. And it is here, at this Council, that this message should mean more than words. Every day, Ukrainians in temporarily occupied regions suffer from the atrocities of the occupation regime. Every day, Ukrainians suffer from Russian attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure. And Ukrainian children have been unlawfully deported and transferred. Beyond Ukraine, Russia keeps violating airspace of other European countries and commits drone incursions in their territories. This illustrates a persistent pattern of irresponsible and escalatory behaviour by Russia. Furthermore, Russia's attacks against Ukraine's ports, shipping, and export infrastructure in the Black Sea continue to endanger freedom of navigation and represent a real threat to global food security. It is clear that Russia's aggression against Ukraine continues to have far-reaching consequences for global security in all its dimensions. And Russia's blatant violations of international law cannot go unanswered. We must show that the international crimes arising from Russia's aggression against Ukraine will not go unpunished, but will instead be met with accountability. Since 2025, we took substantial steps in that direction by establishing the legal foundations for the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine and the Claims Commission. and by continuously supporting the work of the ICC in investigating and prosecuting core international crimes committed in Ukraine. Through these efforts, we are reinforcing the principle that violations of international law must entail consequences, and that accountability is indispensable for a just and lasting peace. Aggression does not pay, and never will. But we must maintain the momentum by continuing to work together to ensure that these mechanisms become operational as soon as possible. The Benelux countries will continue to support Ukraine in its pursuit of justice and call upon the international community to do so too. We welcome genuine efforts towards peace, including ongoing US-led diplomatic efforts. And Ukraine has shown its readiness for peace. Russia must now demonstrate the same through actions, not words. And any peace must be comprehensive, just and lasting, based on the UN Charter and respecting Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine. And the Benelux countries will continue our political, military, humanitarian and financial support to Ukraine. We also remain committed to support Ukraine's recovery, resilience, and reconstruction, as well as addressing the broader humanitarian consequences of this war. A strong Ukraine is essential for sustainable peace, and our support remains unwavering. And our message to Russia is clear: end the aggression now, withdraw your forces from Ukrainian territory, and choose peace. Thank you.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Jetten for his statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Antonio Costa, President of the European Council.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you very much for the opportunity to address the United Nations Security Council today. And let me start by thanking French Presidency for organizing this debate. Since my intervention in the Security Council last year, the human cost of Russia's war has become even more devastating. Every month, thousands of people are killed. Homes, schools, hospitals, energy and water infrastructures are deliberately destroyed in Ukraine. Before the war, Ukraine, the real breadbasket of Europe, fed 400 million people each year around the world through food exports. Now, Russia's strikes on the port of Odessa have created a food security crisis, fueling global inflation with particularly severe consequences for countries across Africa. Russia's attacks on Ukraine also threaten the security of civilians far beyond Ukraine. It is unacceptable that Russia has been threatening the security of European Union member states repeatedly in the past 12 months. This is a dangerous escalation. And last but not least, Russia's revisionist imperial projects have brought death and immense suffering to hundreds of thousands of its own people. And for what? Russia has failed to reach any of its stated goals in this war. The so-called special operation has failed to occupy Ukraine, has failed to impose regime change in Ukraine, and has failed to weaken the determination and unity of Europe to stand with Ukraine. The courage of Ukrainian people has become a symbol across the world for people fighting for their freedom and homeland. Ukraine is defending its cities under constant bombardment and is protecting its sovereignty and independence in the battlefield. Ladies and gentlemen, it is time for this war to end. Escalation and the spreading of the conflict will be disastrous for the international community. The only way forward is diplomacy and the immediate ceasefire. Peace efforts so far have not produced any breakthrough, but we need to persist. The European Union supports all efforts to stop this war. Conditions for a lasting peace are well known. It must respect Ukraine's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and Ukraine's right to choose its own future. In a nutshell, it must respect the United Nations Charter. And it must provide Ukraine with credible security guarantees to ensure a lasting peace. Today, from this Council, I want to make a call to the entire international community to join the European Union in our efforts to bring this war to an end. For this, I ask all of you to use your influence on Russia so that by the time of our meeting next year, we have finally achieved and just and lasting peace in Ukraine and in Europe.
I thank His Excellency Mr. Kurstau for that statement. I now give the floor to His Excellency Mr. Radoslaw Sikorski, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Foreign Affairs of Poland.

Mr. President, please allow me a few extra sentences because I was called out by name by the Foreign Minister of the Russian Federation, and I feel I need to answer. First of all, he calls the events of 2014 in Kiev in Ukraine a bloody coup. I was indeed there with the foreign ministers of Germany and France and there was no coup. The president of Ukraine, Mr. Yanukovych, was voted out of office by a democratically elected parliament of Ukraine, including by his own party of regions. because he carried out a massacre in which 100 or more Ukrainian civilians were killed. Mr. Lavrov also claims, and I quote from the transcript, that in the territory of Ukraine, there's a total ban on the Russian language in all spheres. I was in Kyiv 10 days ago under Russian bombs. and I can assure him that the Russian language is widely spoken there. He is, of course, right that national minorities have the right to speak their language in offices, in courts, in schools. If this is what he demands, then he needs the application of the Council of Europe Convention on the Protection of Minorities. I don't think Ukraine would object to that. and the international community, including Poland, would support that. He has the right to demand the application of that convention. He does not have the right to send tanks and ballistic missiles into Ukraine. Thirdly, he calls the government and the president of Ukraine Nazis. Russian elections to the Duma have also been criticized being not sufficiently democratic. There's a way of resolving it. My proposal is that there should be democratic presidential elections under international supervision in both Russia and Ukraine on the same day. Mr. President, as you said, and as we heard from the briefing by Under Secretary di Carlo and others, Russia is escalating the war. Unable to move forward on the front line, Russia is deliberately targeting Ukrainian civilians, passengers on trains, street vendors, even cyclists, power plants, factories, and shopping malls. The port of Odessa, which, as has been already said, normally exports 50 million tons of grain to Africa and Asia. Russia is now bringing the same tactics into Europe. On September 13, a Russian jet-powered drone hit a Ukrainian train barely two kilometres from a border crossing with Poland. Another followed on the 17th. Drones and missiles have also attacked border crossings with Moldova and Romania. Russia planted an armed drone at Leipzig airport in Germany. Russian drones and aircraft have violated the airspace of, among others, Lithuania, Estonia, Norway and Finland. Russian hit squads have killed people in Spain, Britain, Poland, and Germany. Now they are reaching across the Atlantic. On September 15th, U.S. Attorney's Office here in the Southern District of New York charged members of a Russian intelligence network with, quote, "conspiring to finance terrorism and commit murder for hire in the United States," end quote. cyber attacks, sabotage, clandestine operations, and military pressure. These are not isolated incidents. It's a pattern. Russia is escalating because Russia's leadership is panicking. After more than four years of a senseless colonial war, Vladimir Putin has achieved nothing. He's running out of troops and resources and needs a pretext to mobilize. His unnecessary war has killed or wounded one and a half million Russians. Millions of Ukrainians and other Europeans are increasingly in danger. At any moment, Putin might try to provoke a NATO country and spread the war further, as we have heard from others. To the representatives of the Russian Federation, I have this to say: You have been trying to conquer Donbas for over 12 years and Kyiv for over four. You have been stopped by heroic Ukraine, a country with one-tenth of Russia's GDP. But Poland has almost half of your GDP. Europe has 10 times your GDP. NATO has 25 times your GDP. You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win. You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time. Don't endanger Europe and the world any further. Stop destroying Russia's future. Sergei, I know you're listening. Tell your boss, enough. is enough. Thank you.

I wish to thank his Excellency, Mr. Sikorski, for that statement. A number of speakers remain on my speakers list for this meeting. If the members of the Council agree, I propose that we suspend the meeting until 4:30. The meeting is suspended.
